scenes.tts: A mouse cone is a light-detecting cell of the retina. Its sensitivity resets as the background light brightens. That reset is called adaptation. The textbook account rests on two calcium sensors, the G CAPs and recoverin. Delete both, and the cone still adapts. So what is doing the work?

scenes.visual: A cone cell with two purple sensor chips; a background-light bar brightens and a sensitivity meter falls; both chips are crossed out yet the meter still falls; a dashed question-mark box marks the unknown.
scenes.narration: A mouse cone is a light-detecting cell of the retina. Its sensitivity resets as the background light brightens. That reset is called adaptation. scenes.tts: Light closes channels in the outer segment, so calcium stops entering. A pump keeps removing calcium, so calcium falls. At low calcium, the G CAPs speed c G M P synthesis, which reopens channels. Recoverin lets go of G R K one, the kinase that switches off activated pigment. Both push the cell back toward its dark state while the light stays on. That push is gain control.

scenes.visual: Outer-segment membrane with channel chips; light closes them, calcium dots stop entering, a pump chip removes dots and a calcium gauge falls; GCAP chip sends cGMP to reopen channels; recoverin chip releases a GRK1 chip which acts on an activated-pigment chip; a loop arrow is labelled gain control.

scenes.tts: To test a loop, cut it. Vinberg and Kefalov recorded from isolated mouse retina. The mice also lacked rod transducin, so the signal came from cones. They compared control cones with cones lacking G CAP one, G CAP two and recoverin. The knockout cones still adapted, even with bath calcium lowered to an estimated thirty nanomolar.

scenes.tts: Sensitivity is response size divided by the strength of a dim flash. It falls as the background brightens, and a fit with two numbers describes the fall. I zero is the background that halves sensitivity, and n is the slope. Control cones had I zero of forty-eight thousand eight hundred photons per square micrometre per second, and n of one. Cones lacking the sensors had twelve thousand one hundred, and n of one point five.

Cones lacking the sensors had 12,100, and n of 1.5.
scenes.visual: Log-log axes of relative sensitivity against background; the blue control curve is drawn, then the red knockout curve; half-sensitivity dots mark I0 on each; slope labels appear at high background.

scenes.tts: At a background of forty-eight thousand eight hundred, control cones keep half of their dark sensitivity. Cones lacking the sensors keep about zero point one one, each measured against its own dark sensitivity. To give a response of the same size, they need a flash four point five five times stronger. These are central fit values from mouse cones, ex vivo. So the sensors matter, yet the cones still adapt.
scenes.caption: At a background of 48,800, control cones keep half of their dark sensitivity. Cones lacking the sensors keep about 0.110, each measured against its own dark sensitivity. scenes.tts: The authors read this as a calcium-independent component, and also reported a further calcium-dependent mechanism. But a low-calcium bath changes the solution around the retina. It does not clamp calcium inside the outer segment, and no molecule has been shown to be the residual mechanism. So keep this rule. G CAPs and recoverin contribute, and do not account for all of the adaptation.
